I have seen this means, having pondered my own mind, for my own sake and for yours; our good is common.
mahabharata:12:136.52	For the mongoose and the owl, sitting all around with evil intent, do not dare attack me because of the cat; so I am safe for now.
mahabharata:12:136.53	This owl, crying, with restless eyes, watches me; perched on a branch of the tree, he alarms me greatly.
mahabharata:12:136.54	Friendship of the good is of seven steps; you are my companion, wise one; I shall live with you; you have no fear of death.
mahabharata:12:136.55	For you cannot cut the cat's snare without me; I shall cut your snare, if you do not harm me.
mahabharata:12:136.56	You have resorted to the top of the tree, and I to its root; we two have long lived in this tree, as you know.
mahabharata:12:136.57	The wise do not praise those two, one who is trusted by no one and one who trusts no one anywhere, whose minds are ever agitated.
mahabharata:12:136.58	So let our affection grow, let our alliance be true; the wise do not praise what is past its time and without purpose.
mahabharata:12:136.59	Listen first to this reasoning of interest as it is: I wish for your life, and you wish for mine.
mahabharata:12:136.60	One man crosses a deep great river with a log; he carries the log across, and the log carries him across.
mahabharata:12:136.61	Such will be our union, easy to cross by: I shall carry you across and you will carry me across.
Having spoken thus, Palita, for the sake of the good of both, with reasons that deserved acceptance, looked out for the right moment.
Then hearing his well-spoken words, the shrewd enemy, the cat, spoke words reasoned and worthy of acceptance.
Intelligent and eloquent, going over his words, and seeing that final plight, he honoured him with conciliation alone.
Then the cat Lomasha, sharp-toothed, with eyes like cat's-eye gems, looking gently at the mouse, said:

I am glad, gentle one, good luck to you, who wish me to live; if you know what is best, let it be done; do not hesitate.
mahabharata:12:136.67	I am in firm distress, and you in more distress than I; let an alliance be made between the two of us in distress; do not hesitate.
mahabharata:12:136.68	Do what the time requires, and let our business succeed; once I am freed from this hardship, what you have done will not be lost.
mahabharata:12:136.69	I have laid down my pride, I am your devotee and your disciple, doing what is good for you, subject to your command; I have come to you for refuge.
Thus addressed, Palita, to the cat who had come under his power, spoke these words, beneficial, purposeful and well-shaped.

What you have said is noble; it is no wonder in one like you; but hear the course I know for our good.
mahabharata:12:136.72	I shall come in beneath you; my great fear is the mongoose; save me, do not kill me, and I am able to free you.
mahabharata:12:136.73	And protect me from the owl, for the base creature seeks me; I shall cut your snares, friend; I swear to you by truth.
Hearing those words, apt, fitting and purposeful, Lomasha looked at Palita with joy and welcomed him.
The cat, having honoured Palita, abiding in friendship, the wise one, pleased and in haste, after careful thought spoke:

Come quickly, good luck to you; you are my friend, dear as life; by your grace, wise one, I shall soon regain my life.
mahabharata:12:136.77	Whatever I can do for you now, in this state, command it; I shall do it; let there be an alliance between us, friend.
mahabharata:12:136.78	Freed from this danger, with my friends and kinsmen, I shall do all that is pleasing and beneficial to you.
mahabharata:12:136.79	Freed from this calamity, gentle one, I too may bring you affection and be able to repay you.
Having made the cat grasp his own interest, the mouse then entered, fully trusting, and went about his business properly.
Thus reassured by the cat, the learned mouse, trusting, slept on the cat's chest as on a father's or mother's.
Seeing the mouse nestled against the body of the cat, the mongoose and the owl, disappointed, went to their homes.
But Palita, knowing place and time, nestled against his body, slowly, slowly cut the snares, king, awaiting the right moment.
Then the cat, tormented by his bonds, seeing the mouse cutting the snares without hurry, in haste,
began to urge the unhurried Palita, the mouse, in the cutting of the snares.
Why, gentle one, do you not hurry? Having gained your end, do you despise me? Cut the snares, slayer of foes; the dog-eater will come soon.
Thus urged by him in haste, the wise Palita spoke to the cat, who lacked foresight and was in his power, words for his own good.

Be quiet, gentle one; you need not hurry or panic; we are the ones who know the time here; the time will not be lost.
mahabharata:12:136.89	A task begun at the wrong time does not serve its purpose; the same begun at the right time yields a great purpose.
mahabharata:12:136.90	If you were freed at the wrong time, my fear would be from you alone; so wait for the time; why hurry, friend?
mahabharata:12:136.91	When I see the chandala coming, weapon in hand, then I shall cut your snare, once the common fear has come.
mahabharata:12:136.92	Freed at that time, you will climb the tree, for you will have no other task than your life.
mahabharata:12:136.93	Then when that moment has passed, Lomasha, with you alarmed and frightened, I shall enter my hole, and you will go to the branch.
Thus addressed by the mouse for his own good, the cat, a knower of the truth of words and desirous of life, very wise,
hurried for his own purpose and, behaving with great courtesy, Lomasha spoke to the mouse who was taking his time.

The good do not do the tasks of friends with affection in this way, as I, in haste, delivered you from distress.
mahabharata:12:136.97	In just that same haste you should do what is good for me; make an effort, greatly wise one, that we both may be safe.
mahabharata:12:136.98	Or are you, remembering the old enmity, dragging out the time? See the wickedness of your act; clearly it is the end of my life.
mahabharata:12:136.99	And whatever unpleasant thing I may have done to you before, through ignorance, do not keep it in mind; I ask your pardon; be gracious to me.

A friend who is to be managed as one managed in fear, a friend bound up with fear, must be guarded well, as the hand from a serpent's mouth.
mahabharata:12:136.103	He who, having made an alliance with a stronger one, does not protect himself, finds it like unwholesome food, leading to his ruin.
mahabharata:12:136.104	No one is anyone's friend, no one is anyone's well-wisher; interests are bound by interests, as wild elephants by elephants.
mahabharata:12:136.105	For no one regards the doer once the task is done; therefore one should make all tasks leave something remaining.
mahabharata:12:136.106	And even at that time, you, fearful of fame by day, would be unable to seize me, intent on flight.
mahabharata:12:136.107	The mass of the threads is cut; one thread remains; I shall cut that too, quickly; be at ease, Lomasha.
While the two, both in distress, spoke thus together, that night passed, and fear entered Lomasha.
Then at dawn there appeared a chandala named Parigha, weapon in hand, misshapen, dark-tawny, with heavy hips, gaping, rough, surrounded by a pack of dogs,
with ears like pegs, a huge mouth, grey, of dreadful look.
Seeing him, like a messenger of Yama, the cat, his mind frightened, said to Palita in fear, "What will you do now?"
And the mongoose and the owl, too, greatly terrified at the sight of that dreadful figure, in a moment fell into despair.
Strong and wise, and having come together, they could not be overcome by force, because of the good policy of the two.
Seeing the cat and the mouse who had made an alliance for their purpose, the owl and the mongoose quickly went each to his own dwelling.
Then the mouse cut that thread of the cat; and freed, the cat leapt at once up that very tree.
And the mouse, freed from that fear, freed from the dreadful enemy, entered his hole, and Lomasha took to the branch.
The chandala, taking up his trap and looking all around, his hope destroyed, in a moment withdrew from that place and went to his own house, bull of the Bharatas.
Then, freed from that fear, having regained a life hard to win, the cat on the treetop spoke to Palita in his hole.

Without making any agreement, I was suddenly caught in trouble; do you not suspect me, grateful and well-doing as I am?
mahabharata:12:136.120	Having gained my trust and given me my life, why do you not come near at the time of enjoying a friend's company?
mahabharata:12:136.121	The wrongheaded man who, having first made friends, does not afterwards follow through, gains no friends in hard calamities.
mahabharata:12:136.122	Therefore I was made your friend by you, friend, through your own ability; having become a friend, you should enjoy me.
mahabharata:12:136.123	Whatever friends I have and whatever kinsmen I have, all will honour you, as disciples honour a dear teacher.
mahabharata:12:136.124	And I shall honour you together with your friends and kinsmen; who that is grateful would not honour the giver of life?
mahabharata:12:136.125	Be lord of my body and of my house, and be the governor of all my affairs.
mahabharata:12:136.126	Be my minister, wise one, and rule me like a father; you have no fear from us; I swear by my own life.
mahabharata:12:136.127	In intellect you are Ushanas himself; in strength we are in charge; one joined with your counsel and our strength would surely gain victory.
Thus addressed with the highest conciliation by the cat, the mouse, knowing the highest truth, spoke gentle words for his own good.

All that you have said, Lomasha, I have heard; hear now what occurs to me as I speak.
mahabharata:12:136.130	Friends must be known, and enemies must be understood; this very subtle thing is seen in this world and approved by the wise.
mahabharata:12:136.131	Friends have the form of enemies, and enemies the form of friends; when soothed, they do not notice it, falling under passion and greed.
mahabharata:12:136.132	By birth there is no such thing as an enemy, and no friend exists; friends and enemies are born from the conjunction of capability.
mahabharata:12:136.133	Whoever sees his own interest in another's living, lives so long; he is a friend to him as long as the reverse does not occur.
mahabharata:12:136.134	There is no friendship that is steady, and no ill-will that is certain; by the logic of interests friends and enemies are born.
mahabharata:12:136.135	A friend becomes an enemy in some turn of time, and an enemy becomes a friend, for self-interest is the stronger.
mahabharata:12:136.136	He who trusts friends and does not trust enemies, without understanding the logic of interest, has his life unsteady.
mahabharata:12:136.137	He who, without understanding the logic of interest, sets his mind on the auspicious, whether with a friend or an enemy, has an unsteady mind.
mahabharata:12:136.138	One should not trust the untrustworthy, and even the trustworthy one should not trust fully; fear born of trust cuts even the roots.
mahabharata:12:136.139	By the logic of interests, a father, a mother and sons are pointed out, and maternal uncles, sisters' sons, relatives and kinsmen.
mahabharata:12:136.140	Mother and father abandon a fallen son, though dear, and people protect themselves; see the essential nature of self-interest.
mahabharata:12:136.141	I think you a man of crooked wisdom, who, right after release, look to do a task and seek an easy means, without doubt.
mahabharata:12:136.142	In this very dwelling you were brought down from the banyan, being flighty, not wise, by the trap set before.
mahabharata:12:136.143	One who is flighty is not safe for himself; how will he be for others? Therefore the flighty man surely destroys all tasks.
mahabharata:12:136.144	When someone says sweetly, 'You are dear to me,' all that is a false pretence; hear me out at length.
mahabharata:12:136.145	By a cause one becomes dear, by a cause one becomes hated; this world of the living is intent on interest; no one is dear to anyone.
mahabharata:12:136.146	Friendship between brothers of the same womb, or between husband and wife, I do not know to be causeless affection anywhere here.
mahabharata:12:136.147	Even if brothers or wives are angry for some other reason, they are loved by nature; other people are not loved so.
mahabharata:12:136.148	One becomes dear by giving, another by pleasant speech, another by mantras, oblations and recitations; people are loved for the sake of a purpose.
mahabharata:12:136.149	When a cause arose, there was affection between us; when the cause is gone, that affection turns back, once the ground of the cause is destroyed.
mahabharata:12:136.150	What cause do I think there is by which I would be dear to you, other than as food? And even there we are wise.
mahabharata:12:136.151	Time alters the cause, self-interest follows it; the wise man knows his interest, and the world follows the wise.
mahabharata:12:136.152	Such a thing should not be said by you to one who is learned and skilled in his own interest; in a time not out of joint, this is your motive of self-interest.
mahabharata:12:136.153	So I do not stray from my own interest, being firm in peace and war; the forms of clouds change from moment to moment.
mahabharata:12:136.154	On this very day an enemy, and again on this very day a friend, and again on this very day an enemy; see the fickleness of arrangements.
mahabharata:12:136.155	Our friendship lasted only as long as the cause existed before; it has gone with that cause, joined to the time.
mahabharata:12:136.156	You are my utter enemy, who became a friend through necessity; that task is accomplished, and the nature has turned to enmity.
mahabharata:12:136.157	Knowing thus the shastras as they were laid down, in truth, how could I enter a snare of your making? Tell me that.
mahabharata:12:136.158	I was freed by your strength, and you by mine; once mutual favour is done, there is no further meeting.
mahabharata:12:136.159	You, gentle one, have gained your end today, and we have accomplished ours; you have no other business with me than eating me.
mahabharata:12:136.160	I am food, you the eater; I am weak and you strong; there is no alliance between us when strength is unequal and bound to a task.
mahabharata:12:136.161	I admire your wisdom, that right after release you seek food, surely an easy means, without doubt.
mahabharata:12:136.162	Bound only for the sake of food, you, freed and hungry, having plotted, surely mean to eat me today, a knower of the shastras.
mahabharata:12:136.163	I know you are hungry, and it is your mealtime; having plotted so, you seek food again.
mahabharata:12:136.164	And as for the wife and sons you entrust to me, my friend, it is not fitting that I should serve them.
mahabharata:12:136.165	Seeing me with you, your dear wife and sons, delighted and fond of you, why would they not eat me?
mahabharata:12:136.166	I shall not come together with you; the reason for our meeting is past; think of my welfare from where you are, if good deeds are remembered.
mahabharata:12:136.167	What wise man would go within the reach of an enemy who is troubled and hungry, seeking food, when he himself would be that food?
mahabharata:12:136.168	Good luck to you; I shall go; I fear you even from afar; I shall not come together with you; be at peace, Lomasha.
mahabharata:12:136.169	For nearness to the strong is never praised; even of one who is calm I must, wise one, always be afraid, if he is strong.
mahabharata:12:136.170	But if you have need of my wealth, say what I shall do; I shall give everything you wish, but never myself.
mahabharata:12:136.171	For one's own sake offspring may be given up, and kingdom, jewels and wealth; giving up even everything, one should protect oneself by oneself.
mahabharata:12:136.172	For those who hold lordship, wealth and jewels even in the hands of an enemy, return has been seen; but life, we have heard, does not return.
mahabharata:12:136.173	But the giving of oneself is not wished for like that of wealth and jewels; the self must be protected from every side, even at the cost of wives and riches.
mahabharata:12:136.174	For those who guard themselves and act after careful examination, calamities born of their own faults do not arise.
mahabharata:12:136.175	Weak ones who rightly know their stronger enemies, their minds, resolved for their own good, are not shaken.
Thus plainly rebuked by Palita, the cat, ashamed, spoke to the mouse these words:

I admire your wisdom, since you, intent on my good, spoke in the truth of interest, while I was of confused sight.
mahabharata:12:136.178	But you ought not to know me otherwise, good one; the friendship I have from you has come from the gift of life.
mahabharata:12:136.179	I am a knower of dharma, a knower of virtues, and above all grateful; I am affectionate to friends, especially to those like you.
mahabharata:12:136.180	So, good one, in this state, you should not hold me off; if driven off by you, I would give up my life with my kinsmen.
mahabharata:12:136.181	The wise have seen the word 'shame' used of high-minded ones like me; death is better; knower of the truth of dharma, you should not suspect me.
Thus praised by the cat, the mouse, in his mind deep in feeling, spoke to the cat:

You are good, and I have learned the matter; I am pleased, but I do not trust; neither by praises nor by floods of wealth can I be won again by you.
mahabharata:12:136.184	For the wise, friend, do not fall into the power of an enemy without cause; on this subject hear two verses made by Ushanas.
mahabharata:12:136.185	In a task common to enemies, having made an alliance with a stronger one, one should act collected, by sound method, and once the end is gained, not trust him.
mahabharata:12:136.186	Therefore in all circumstances one should protect one's life; wealth and offspring and all belong to the living.
mahabharata:12:136.187	The essence of the policy-shastras is held to be distrust above all; therefore among men distrust is ample benefit to oneself.
mahabharata:12:136.188	The distrustful are not slain by enemies, even if weak, but the trusting, even if strong, are quickly slain by the weak.
mahabharata:12:136.189	From those like you I must always guard myself, cat; and you too guard yourself from the chandala, from his low birth's stain.
As he spoke thus, the cat, struck with fear and alarm, went off at speed from there to his own place.
Then Palita, wise, knowing the truth of the shastras, having made known the power of his own intellect, went to another hole.
Thus, by wise intelligence, a weak but wise man should make an alliance with many mighty enemies, even alone.
A wise man should make peace even with a capable enemy; the mouse and the cat were both freed by relying on each other.
So this path of kshatriya dharma has been shown by me at length, king; hear it again in brief.
Those two, who had made enmity with each other, made the highest affection, and each had the thought of outwitting the other.
There the wise one outwits, properly, by the strength of his intellect; the wise is outwitted through negligence even by the unwise.
Therefore, fearful, one should act as if not afraid, and not trusting, as if trusting; for the careful one does not stumble, and the one who stumbles perishes.
Peace with an enemy in due time, war with a friend in due time: so the knowers of truth have ever said, Yudhishthira.
Thinking thus, great king, and having mastered the meaning of the shastras, one who is attacked should be careful, and before the danger come, act as if afraid.
One should make provision as if afraid, and counter-alliance likewise; from fear arises a wisdom born of watchful effort.
There is no fear, king, for the one who fears when the danger has not come; but for the fearless, from overconfidence, a very great fear arises.
One should never reveal counsel on the ground that someone is not timid; for from ignorance, once it is known, it would reach those who show the weak points."
Hearing this, find peace; do not be absorbed in worry, king; know, bull among men, that the three worlds rest on one's own deeds.
In radiance like the sun, in forbearance like the earth, in intellect like Brihaspati, steady like the Himalaya,
Those who wronged Draupadi and took your sovereignty, those cruel ones, have passed away, slain in battle in accordance with dharma.
And Hrishikesha ran then toward Yuyudhana, who was likewise striking others on every side, wishing to restrain him.

[Indra said:] "Krodhavasha demons seize what is given, offered, laid open and poured in oblation when a dog has seen it; therefore abandon this dog; by abandoning the dog you will reach the world of the gods."
I will not go there; let it be reported that I am staying; by my presence, messenger, these brothers of mine are happy.
